notes.note: Dio shows Caesar's reaction to Cleopatra's death after the Egyptian campaign: admiration and pity, and grief as if robbed of the glory of victory. This is not a claim about the Battle of Actium itself.
notes.quotation: felt both admiration and pity for her, and was excessively grieved on his own account

notes.note: Dio's summary judgement of Antony's character as a string of contradictions (wise yet foolish, brave yet cowardly); it bears on how the source understands his conduct in the war, including Actium, but states no event.
notes.quotation: Antony had no superior in comprehending his duty, yet he committed many acts of folly.

notes.note: Dio's summary judgment of Cleopatra's character and of her fall, drawn from the passage on the end of the war; it states no event of the battle itself.
notes.quotation: Cleopatra was of insatiable passion and insatiable avarice; she was swayed often by laudable ambition, but often by overweening effrontery.

notes.note: Dio reads Cleopatra's hope of becoming Queen of the Romans as the cause of her ruin, but the passage names no one and no event.
notes.quotation: By love she gained the title of Queen of the Egyptians, and when she hoped by the same means to win also that of Queen of the Romans, she failed of this and lost the other besides.
